facts.title: Forged in Darmstadt, 1994
facts.text: Darmstadtium was first created on 9 November 1994 at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany. A team led by Sigurd Hofmann and Peter Armbruster fused lead-208 with nickel-62 nuclei accelerated to enormous speeds. Only a single atom of darmstadtium-269 was detected in that first run, identified by the chain of alpha particles it emitted as it decayed.

facts.title: Named for a German city
facts.text: The element takes its name from Darmstadt, the city where it was discovered, making it one of the few elements named after the specific town of its creation rather than a country or person. The name was officially approved by IUPAC in 2003. Before that, it carried the placeholder systematic name ununnilium (Uun), simply meaning 'one-one-zero' in Latin-Greek numbering.

facts.title: An atom-by-atom element
facts.text: Darmstadtium has never been produced in weighable amounts; scientists have only ever made a few dozen atoms total. Creating it requires firing trillions of projectile ions at a target for days or weeks just to score one successful fusion event. This is why almost everything we 'know' about it is inferred from theory and the behaviour of lighter relatives like platinum, not from direct measurement of a sample.

facts.title: Vanishes in a flash
facts.text: Every isotope of darmstadtium is intensely radioactive and decays almost instantly. Its most stable known isotope, darmstadtium-281, has a half-life of only about 11 seconds, while the original Ds-269 lasted under a thousandth of a second. Because it disappears so fast, no one will ever hold a visible piece of it.

facts.title: Predicted to be ultra-dense
facts.text: Although a real lump has never existed, calculations suggest darmstadtium would be one of the densest substances imaginable, with an estimated density around 26 to 34 grams per cubic centimetre. That is roughly 1.5 times denser than gold or lead. The huge density comes from packing 110 protons and many neutrons into each tiny, heavy nucleus.

facts.title: Platinum's heavy cousin
facts.text: Darmstadtium sits directly below platinum, palladium and nickel in group 10 of the periodic table, so chemists expect it to behave like a noble, unreactive transition metal. If a sample could ever be assembled, it would likely be a silvery or grey solid that resists corrosion. Relativistic effects on its fast-moving inner electrons, however, might make its chemistry subtly different from platinum's.

facts.title: A doorway to superheavies
facts.text: Darmstadtium was a crucial stepping stone in the race to fill the bottom of the periodic table. The same GSI 'cold fusion' technique that produced it was used to discover its neighbours roentgenium (111) and copernicium (112) within just two years. Each new element pushed scientists closer to the theorised 'island of stability,' a region where superheavy nuclei might survive much longer.

facts.title: Born only in laboratories
facts.text: Darmstadtium does not occur anywhere in nature, not on Earth, in meteorites, or in stars. Any darmstadtium that might have formed in violent cosmic events like neutron-star collisions would have decayed away in seconds, long before it could be detected. It is a purely synthetic, human-made element that exists only when a particle accelerator manufactures it.

facts.title: Read by its decay signature
facts.text: Because you cannot see or weigh a single atom, scientists identify darmstadtium by the unique 'fingerprint' of radiation it leaves behind. The atom emits a precise sequence of alpha particles, each with a characteristic energy, as it transforms step-by-step into lighter known elements. Matching that decay chain to predictions is how the GSI team proved they had truly made element 110.

facts.title: No jobs, only knowledge
facts.text: Darmstadtium has zero industrial, medical, or biological uses, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its entire value is scientific: studying how it forms and decays tests our theories of nuclear structure and the limits of the periodic table. In that sense it is a pure 'curiosity' element, made to answer the question of how big an atom can get.
